claim: SWI/SNF-family chromatin remodeling complexes, such as S. cerevisiae RSC, slide and eject nucleosomes to regulate transcription.
source: SWI/SNF-family chromatin remodeling complexes, such as S. cerevisiae RSC, slide and eject nucleosomes to regulate transcription.
evidence: This is a general statement about the function of SWI/SNF-family complexes, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Within nucleosomes, stiff DNA sequences confer spontaneous partial unwrapping.
source: Within nucleosomes, stiff DNA sequences confer spontaneous partial unwrapping, prompting whether and how SWI/SNF-family remodelers are specialized to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about DNA-nucleosome interactions and biophysical properties of DNA sequences.

claim: RSC1 and RSC2 are orthologs of mammalian PBRM1 (polybromo) which define two separate RSC sub-complexes.
source: RSC1 and RSC2 are orthologs of mammalian PBRM1 (polybromo) which define two separate RSC sub-complexes.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary relationship and structural organization of RSC complexes, based on established knowledge.

claim: In vitro, the Rsc1-containing complex remodels partially-unwrapped nucleosomes much better than does the Rsc2-containing complex.
source: Remarkably, in vitro the Rsc1-containing complex remodels partially-unwrapped nucleosomes much better than does the Rsc2-containing complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro remodeling assays presented in the manuscript (e.g., Figure 2C, Figure 3E).

claim: A rsc1Δ mutation, but not rsc2Δ, is lethal with histone mutations that confer partial unwrapping.
source: Moreover, a rsc1Δ mutation, but not rsc2Δ, is lethal with histone mutations that confer partial unwrapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic screen data presented in the manuscript (Table 1, Figure 3A).

claim: Rsc1/2 isoforms both cooperate with the DNA-binding proteins Rsc3/30 and the HMG protein, Hmo1, to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, but show differential reliance on these factors.
source: Rsc1/2 isoforms both cooperate with the DNA-binding proteins Rsc3/30 and the HMG protein, Hmo1, to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, but show differential reliance on these factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4C), in vitro remodeling assays with Hmo1 (Figure 4D), and genetic interaction studies (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Genetic impairment of Rsc1/2, Rsc3/30, and Hmo1 strongly reduces the expression of genes with wide nucleosome-deficient regions (e.g., ribosomal protein genes), known to harbor partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
source: Notably, genetic impairment of these factors strongly reduces the expression of genes with wide nucleosome-deficient regions (e.g., ribosomal protein genes), known to harbor partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing downregulation of ribosomal protein genes in double mutants (Figure 5G-H).

claim: Rsc1/2 isoforms are specialized through composition and interactions to manage and remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
source: Taken together, Rsc1/2 isoforms are specialized through composition and interactions to manage and remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript, including biochemical, genetic, and genomic data.

claim: Nucleosomes regulate transcription in diverse ways and can either block or attract transcriptional regulators.
source: Nucleosomes regulate transcription in diverse ways and can either block or attract transcriptional regulators (Workman and Kingston, 1998; Iyer, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: At promoters, nucleosome positioning and/or occupancy plays a central role in regulating transcription factor binding, with transitions in nucleosome positioning typically accompanying activation.
source: At promoters, nucleosome positioning and/or occupancy plays a central role in regulating transcription factor binding, with transitions in nucleosome positioning typically accompanying activation.
evidence: This is a general statement about nucleosome function at promoters, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: SWI/SNF-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes (CRCs) have evolved to conduct nucleosome sliding and ejection, and enable transcription factor access to DNA.
source: SWI/SNF-family ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes (CRCs) have evolved to conduct nucleosome sliding and ejection, and enable transcription factor access to DNA.
evidence: This is a general statement about the function of SWI/SNF-family complexes, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: SWI/SNF-family CRCs utilize a catalytic ATPase to translocate DNA around nucleosomes to conduct nucleosome sliding and eviction, and contain an additional set of proteins to help target and regulate each complex.
source: These CRCs are complex in both composition and mechanism; they utilize a catalytic ATPase to translocate DNA around nucleosomes to conduct nucleosome sliding and eviction, and contain an additional set of proteins to help target and regulate each complex (Clapier and Cairns, 2009; Lorch and Kornberg, 2017; Narlikar et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work describing the mechanism and composition of chromatin remodeling complexes.

claim: RSC (Remodels the Structure of Chromatin) from the budding yeast S. cerevisiae is both essential and abundant, and has long served as a prototype CRC.
source: The SWI/SNF-family remodeler, RSC (Remodels the Structure of Chromatin), from the budding yeast S. cerevisiae, is both essential and abundant, and has long served as a prototype CRC.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties and role of RSC in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: RSC complex is found in more than one compositional subtype, and contains either Rsc1 or its highly-related paralog, Rsc2.
source: RSC complex (like others in the SWI/SNF family) is found in more than one compositional subtype, and contains either Rsc1 or its highly-related paralog, Rsc2 (Cairns et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing RSC composition.

claim: Rsc1 and Rsc2 are orthologs of the mammalian polybromo, as both contain multiple bromodomains, a bromodomain-adjacent homology (BAH) domain, and a DNA binding motif (AT Hook or HMG box).
source: Rsc1 and Rsc2 are orthologs of the mammalian polybromo, as both contain multiple bromodomains, a bromodomain-adjacent homology (BAH) domain, and a DNA binding motif (AT Hook or HMG box).
evidence: This is a statement about the domain structure and evolutionary relationship of Rsc1/2 and polybromo, based on established knowledge.

claim: Additional RSC compositional variation has been suggested, involving the association of two additional paralogous RSC subunits, Rsc3 and Rsc30.
source: Additional RSC compositional variation has been suggested, involving the association of two additional paralogous RSC subunits, Rsc3 and Rsc30 (Campsteijn et al., 2007; Chambers et al., 2012), which are zinc cluster DNA-binding proteins with affinity for GC-rich sequences (Badis et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing RSC composition and Rsc3/30 function.

claim: Rsc3 and Rsc30 are zinc cluster DNA-binding proteins with affinity for GC-rich sequences.
source: Additional RSC compositional variation has been suggested, involving the association of two additional paralogous RSC subunits, Rsc3 and Rsc30 (Campsteijn et al., 2007; Chambers et al., 2012), which are zinc cluster DNA-binding proteins with affinity for GC-rich sequences (Badis et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing Rsc3/30 DNA-binding properties.

claim: RSC1 and RSC2 are redundant for viability (rsc1Δ rsc2Δ mutants are inviable).
source: RSC1 and RSC2 are redundant for viability (rsc1Δ rsc2Δ mutants are inviable), however loss of only one confers mild but dissimilar phenotypes, suggesting overlapping essential functions alongside limited unique functions (Baetz et al., 2004; Chambers et al., 2012; Cairns et al., 1999; Bungard et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing the genetic properties of rsc1 and rsc2 mutants.

claim: Loss of only one of RSC1 or RSC2 confers mild but dissimilar phenotypes, suggesting overlapping essential functions alongside limited unique functions.
source: RSC1 and RSC2 are redundant for viability (rsc1Δ rsc2Δ mutants are inviable), however loss of only one confers mild but dissimilar phenotypes, suggesting overlapping essential functions alongside limited unique functions (Baetz et al., 2004; Chambers et al., 2012; Cairns et al., 1999; Bungard et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and represents an inference about the functional relationship between Rsc1 and Rsc2.

claim: Partially-unwrapped nucleosomes are defined as those in which the DNA has released (or displays a tendency to release) from the histone octamer at one or both of the symmetric locations where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome, while the central DNA gyre maintains association with the octamer.
source: Partially-unwrapped nucleosomes are defined here as those in which the DNA has released (or displays a tendency to release) from the histone octamer at one or both of the symmetric locations where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome, while the central DNA gyre maintains association with the octamer.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors to clarify terminology used in the manuscript.

claim: DNA sequences differ in their affinity for histone octamers and propensity to form nucleosomes.
source: DNA sequences differ in their affinity for histone octamers and propensity to form nucleosomes (Anderson et al., 2002); stiff homopolymer AT tracts deter nucleosome formation (Segal and Widom, 2009) whereas those with short (5 bp) alternating AT and GC tracts more easily adopt nucleosomal curvature, providing a lower cost in energy for nucleosome formation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing DNA sequence effects on nucleosome formation.

claim: Stiff homopolymer AT tracts deter nucleosome formation.
source: DNA sequences differ in their affinity for histone octamers and propensity to form nucleosomes (Anderson et al., 2002); stiff homopolymer AT tracts deter nucleosome formation (Segal and Widom, 2009) whereas those with short (5 bp) alternating AT and GC tracts more easily adopt nucleosomal curvature, providing a lower cost in energy for nucleosome formation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA sequences with short (5 bp) alternating AT and GC tracts more easily adopt nucleosomal curvature, providing a lower cost in energy for nucleosome formation.
source: DNA sequences differ in their affinity for histone octamers and propensity to form nucleosomes (Anderson et al., 2002); stiff homopolymer AT tracts deter nucleosome formation (Segal and Widom, 2009) whereas those with short (5 bp) alternating AT and GC tracts more easily adopt nucleosomal curvature, providing a lower cost in energy for nucleosome formation.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about DNA biophysical properties and nucleosome formation.

claim: The commonly used '601' nucleosome positioning sequence is synthetic, was selected for high affinity, and displays a 5 bp AT/GC alternating pattern.
source: The commonly used '601' nucleosome positioning sequence is synthetic, was selected for high affinity (Lowary and Widom, 1998), and displays a 5 bp AT/GC alternating pattern.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the work that developed the 601 sequence.

claim: The 5S rRNA gene sequence is naturally occurring and of lesser affinity (comparable to genome averages) in comparison to 601.
source: In contrast, the 5S rRNA gene sequence is naturally occurring and of lesser affinity (comparable to genome averages) in comparison to 601 (Polach and Widom, 1995; Dong et al., 1990; Li and Widom, 2004; Zhou et al., 2019; Mauney et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work comparing the 5S and 601 sequences.

claim: Recent work using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) with salt titration demonstrates that the 5S nucleosome unwraps more rapidly and at lower salt concentrations than the 601 nucleosome.
source: However, recent work using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) with salt titration to compare the unwrapping dynamics of the 5S and 601 nucleosomes demonstrates that the 5S nucleosome unwraps more rapidly and at lower salt concentrations than the 601 nucleosome (Mauney et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work using SAXS to study nucleosome unwrapping.

claim: Prior work has revealed the presence of partially-unwrapped 'fragile' nucleosomes at promoters with an especially wide nucleosome deficient region (NDR), and co-incidence of RSC, including at the majority of ribosomal protein genes (RPGs).
source: Prior work has revealed the presence of partially-unwrapped 'fragile' nucleosomes at promoters with an especially wide nucleosome deficient region (NDR), and co-incidence of RSC, including at the majority of ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) (Kubik et al., 2015; Brahma and Henikoff, 2019; Knight et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing nucleosome occupancy and RSC localization at promoters.

claim: In silico size fractionation of RSC-bound nucleosomes provides evidence that RSC occupies wrapped nucleosomes at the +1 and −1 promoter positions, as well as a partially-unwrapped nucleosome interposed between those two displaying lower/fractional occupancy – the basis for the appearance of a large NDR.
source: Indeed, in silico size fractionation of RSC-bound nucleosomes provides evidence that RSC occupies wrapped nucleosomes at the +1 and −1 promoter positions, as well as a partially-unwrapped nucleosome interposed between those two displaying lower/fractional occupancy – the basis for the appearance of a large NDR (Brahma and Henikoff, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work analyzing RSC-bound nucleosomes.

claim: Partially-unwrapped nucleosomes are likely conformationally diverse.
source: As partially-unwrapped nucleosomes are likely conformationally diverse (Bilokapic et al., 2018), RSC may have evolved to both recognize and remodel these nucleosomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and represents an inference about nucleosome conformational diversity.

claim: RSC may have evolved to both recognize and remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
source: As partially-unwrapped nucleosomes are likely conformationally diverse (Bilokapic et al., 2018), RSC may have evolved to both recognize and remodel these nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary specialization of RSC.

claim: Prior work with the Rsc2-containing form of RSC revealed altered remodeling outcomes for partially-unwrapped (H3 R40A) nucleosomes.
source: Prior work with the Rsc2-containing form of RSC revealed altered remodeling outcomes for partially-unwrapped (H3 R40A) nucleosomes (Somers and Owen-Hughes, 2009), further questioning whether an alternative form of RSC might better manage them.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rsc3/30 heterodimer preferentially associates with the RSC1 complex via the CT2 domain.
source: The Rsc3/30 heterodimer preferentially associates with the RSC1 complex via the CT2 domain
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TAP purifications (Figure 1A-B), stringency testing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and domain swap experiments (Figure 1C-E).

claim: Rsc1 and Rsc2 are highly similar proteins (45% identical, 62% similar), with high homology present in the bromodomains, BAH domain, and the CT1 region.
source: Rsc1 and Rsc2 are highly similar proteins (45% identical, 62% similar), with high homology present in the bromodomains, BAH domain, and the CT1 region – whereas the CT2 region, which is required for Rsc1 or Rsc2 assembly into RSC, is considerably more divergent (Cairns et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is based on sequence comparison and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The CT2 region of Rsc1/2, which is required for Rsc1 or Rsc2 assembly into RSC, is considerably more divergent between Rsc1 and Rsc2.
source: Rsc1 and Rsc2 are highly similar proteins (45% identical, 62% similar), with high homology present in the bromodomains, BAH domain, and the CT1 region – whereas the CT2 region, which is required for Rsc1 or Rsc2 assembly into RSC, is considerably more divergent (Cairns et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is based on sequence comparison and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rsc3/30 is present at apparent stoichiometric levels in the Rsc1-containing complex, but substoichiometric levels in the Rsc2-containing complex.
source: To determine, we purified RSC sub-complexes using a TAP tag (Puig et al., 2001) on either Rsc1 or Rsc2, which revealed Rsc3/30 at apparent stoichiometric levels in the Rsc1-containing complex, but substoichiometric levels in the Rsc2-containing complex (Figure 1A and B; Chambers et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TAP purifications shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: When purifications were conducted under increasing salt conditions, Rsc3/30 association with Rsc1-TAP was maintained, but was lost with Rsc2-TAP, confirming higher avidity of Rsc3/30 for the Rsc1 sub-type.
source: Furthermore, when purifications were conducted under increasing salt conditions, Rsc3/30 association with Rsc1-TAP was maintained, but was lost with Rsc2-TAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) confirming higher avidity of Rsc3/30 for the Rsc1 sub-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from stringency testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CT2 domain of Rsc1 mediates preferential association with Rsc3/30.
source: To identify whether a particular region within Rsc1 mediates this preferential association with Rsc3/30, we performed domain swaps between Rsc1 and Rsc2 (Figure 1C) and checked for complementation and Rsc3 association.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments and co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 1C-E).

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation revealed strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1, and with Rsc2 derivatives only if they contained the CT2 region of Rsc1.
source: Here, co-immunoprecipitation revealed strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1, and with Rsc2 derivatives only if they contained the CT2 region of Rsc1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1 was lost when Rsc1 contained the CT2 region of Rsc2.
source: Conversely, strong Rsc3 association with Rsc1 was lost when Rsc1 contained the CT2 region of Rsc2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The region on Rsc1 responsible for strong Rsc3/30 association is narrowed to residues 617–777.
source: Similar approaches involving internal Rsc1/2 deletions and additional swap positions provided further refinement, narrowing the region on Rsc1 responsible for strong Rsc3/30 association to residues 617–777 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deletion and domain swap experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Several structures of RSC-nucleosome complexes have recently been published.
source: Several structures of RSC-nucleosome complexes have recently been published (Wagner et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Rsc1, Rsc2, Rsc3, and Rsc30 are within the flexible regions of RSC-nucleosome structures, and these structures contain only partial models (or lack density/models).
source: However, as Rsc1, Rsc2, Rsc3, and Rsc30 are within the flexible regions, these structures contain only partial models (or lack density/models).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of published structures and represents an inference about the structural flexibility of these subunits.

claim: While the Rsc1-Rsc3/30 interaction has not been resolved structurally, crosslinks were observed between Rsc2 CT2 and Rsc3/30 heterodimer.
source: While the Rsc1-Rsc3/30 interaction has not been resolved structurally, crosslinks were observed between Rsc2 CT2 and Rsc3/30 heterodimer (Wagner et al., 2020), an interaction we find to be much stronger in Rsc1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and by the experimental data presented in this manuscript.

claim: All four RSC complexes (RSC1+3/30, RSC1-3/30, RSC2+3/30, RSC2-3/30) displayed similar DNA-dependent ATPase activities in typical Vmax determinations with plasmid DNA.
source: First, all four RSC complexes displayed similar DNA-dependent ATPase activities in typical Vmax determinations with plasmid DNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The activity of RSC1-3/30 complex plateaued earlier than the other RSC complexes in ATPase assays.
source: The activity of one complex, RSC1-3/30, plateaued earlier than the other RSC complexes, but otherwise the two complexes behaved similarly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RSC1 complex displayed much greater sliding activity than RSC2 on 5S nucleosomes.
source: However, major differences were observed with 5S nucleosomes – RSC1 complex displayed much greater sliding activity than RSC2 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for quantification).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All sliding activities with RSC1 and RSC2 complexes are ATP dependent.
source: As shown previously for RSC, all sliding activities with RSC1 and RSC2 complexes are ATP dependent (Cairns et al., 1996 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP.
source: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) indicating that their differences in activities occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The differences in remodeling activities between RSC1 and RSC2 complexes occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
source: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both bound 5S nucleosomes comparably in the absence of ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) indicating that their differences in activities occur after the initial engagement of the 5S nucleosome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RSC1 and RSC2 bind nucleosomes similarly but remodel them differently.

claim: The Rsc3/30 module did not affect ATPase activities of RSC1 or RSC2 complexes.
source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Rsc3/30 module did not affect binding of RSC1 or RSC2 complexes to 5S nucleosomes.
source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling of 5S nucleosomes.
source: Finally, the Rsc3/30 module did not affect their ATPase activities (Figure 2B) nor their binding to 5S nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B); however, in both the RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, Rsc3/30 inclusion moderately inhibited remodeling (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The slower-migrating RSC remodeled product on native gels is an intact nucleosome, not a hexasome or tetrasome.
source: Here, the 'slid' band maintained a dimer to DNA ratio similar to the starting nucleosome, rather than that predicted for a hexasome or tetrasome, supporting the identity of the slower-migrating band being an intact nucleosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sliding assays with fluorescently labeled H2A shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Histone mutations that are lethal specifically with rsc1Δ mapped exclusively within the H3 αN helix region – the position where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome.
source: In striking contrast, those mutations that were lethal specifically with rsc1Δ mapped exclusively within the H3 αN helix region – the position where DNA enters/exits the nucleosome (Table 1, Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Table 1 and Figure 3A-B.

claim: The specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in the screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats.
source: Furthermore, the specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in our screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats (Ferreira et al., 2007), whereas alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the genetic screen data with published FRET data, shown in Table 2.

claim: Alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype in the genetic screen (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping.
source: Furthermore, the specific H3 αN helix mutations obtained in our screen overlap strongly with those reported to increase partial unwrapping using FRET formats (Ferreira et al., 2007), whereas alanine substitutions that did not show a phenotype (P43A, E50A, K56A) had little effect on FRET/unwrapping (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the genetic screen data with published FRET data, shown in Table 2.

claim: rsc1Δ shows synthetic lethality primarily with mutations in the H2A C-terminus which interact with the H3 αN helix, as well as with specific histone-DNA contacts (H2A R78 and H2A R30).
source: In keeping with the results above, we find rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethality primarily with mutations in the H2A C-terminus which interact with the H3 αN helix, as well as with specific histone-DNA contacts (H2A R78 and H2A R30; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens with H2A-H2B mutations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Synthetic lethality in rsc1∆ strains is due to decreased ability of RSC2 complexes to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes relative to RSC1 complexes.
source: Taken together, our genetic results, which encompass the entire nucleosome, strongly suggest that synthetic lethality in rsc1∆ strains is due to decreased ability of RSC2 complexes to remodel partially-unwrapped nucleosomes relative to RSC1 complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic screen data showing that rsc1Δ-specific synthetic lethal mutations map to regions involved in DNA entry/exit from the nucleosome.

claim: The CT2 domain of Rsc1, which interacts better with Rsc3/30 than its counterpart in Rsc2, confers growth when placed within a Rsc2 derivative in combination with histone αN helix mutations.
source: Here, growth was clearly restored to rsc1Δ H3 G44A and rsc1Δ H3 R40A combinations with a plasmid encoding Rsc1 or Rsc2 bearing the Rsc1 CT2, but not with Rsc2 or Rsc1 bearing the Rsc2 CT2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from complementation assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Additional domain swap experiments localize the complementation of rsc1Δ αN helix histone combined lethality to the Rsc3/30 association region in Rsc1 (aa 617–777).
source: Additional domain swap experiments localize this complementation to the Rsc3/30 association region in Rsc1 (aa 617–777) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: High-copy RSC3 or RSC30 suppresses the strong temperature sensitivity (Ts-) phenotype of rsc1Δ H3 V46A.
source: While high-copy RSC3 or RSC30 could not rescue rsc1Δ αN helix histone combined lethality (data not shown), suppression of the strong temperature sensitivity (Ts-) phenotype of rsc1Δ H3 V46A was observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from high-copy suppression assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Improving the association/functionality of Rsc3/30 suppresses phenotypes associated with αN helix histone mutations.
source: Taken together, improving the association/functionality of Rsc3/30 suppresses phenotypes associated with αN helix histone mutations – further linking Rsc1/2 and Rsc3/30 to partial nucleosome unwrapping.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the complementation and suppression experiments.

claim: The H3 K56A mutation was not lethal in combination with either rsc1Δ or rsc2Δ.
source: However, the H3 K56A mutation was not lethal in combination with either rsc1Δ or rsc2Δ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The H3 K56Q mutation confers synthetic lethality when combined with rsc1Δ, but not with rsc2Δ.
source: The K56Q mutation confers synthetic lethality when combined with rsc1Δ, but not with rsc2Δ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Domain swaps involving the highly homologous bromodomains and BAH domains between Rsc1 and Rsc2 did not confer phenotypic differences, nor did these swaps alter the synthetic lethality of rsc1Δ with histone αN helix mutations.
source: Furthermore, domain swaps involving the highly homologous bromodomains and BAH domains between Rsc1 and Rsc2 did not confer phenotypic differences, nor did these swaps alter the synthetic lethality of rsc1Δ with histone αN helix mutations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from domain swap experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: H3 K56A has little effect on DNA unwrapping, whereas K56Q promotes unwrapping.
source: Notably, H3 K56A has little effect on DNA unwrapping, whereas K56Q promotes unwrapping (Ferreira et al., 2007; Masumoto et al., 2005) – and is lethal with rsc1Δ, further supporting an unwrapping function as being responsible for the phenotype.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and by the genetic data presented in this manuscript.

claim: The lethality of H3 K56Q with rsc1Δ does not appear linked to bromodomains or histone acetylation.
source: Thus, the lethality with rsc1Δ does not appear linked to bromodomains or histone acetylation, in agreement with findings that H3K56 acetylation does not enhance RSC binding (Neumann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain swap experiments and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Although sliding of nucleosomes bearing H3 R40A by either form of RSC is reduced relative to wild-type (WT) 5S nucleosomes, RSC1 complexes were markedly more active than RSC2 complexes.
source: Although sliding of nucleosomes bearing H3 R40A by either form of RSC is reduced relative to wild-type (WT) 5S nucleosomes, RSC1 complexes were markedly more active than RSC2 complexes (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for quantification), reinforcing the difference between RSC1 and RSC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly.
source: Additionally, both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by this octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome binding assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by the H3 R40A octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
source: Additionally, both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes bind H3 αN helix mutant 5S nucleosomes similarly (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that initial nucleosome binding is not inhibited by this octamer mutation, suggesting downstream remodeling activity as the affected step.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that RSC1 and RSC2 bind H3 R40A nucleosomes similarly but remodel them differently.

claim: WT 174 bp 5S yeast nucleosomes display a fully-wrapped side (position 158), and a side of partial unwrapping, in agreement with asymmetric 5S nucleosome unwrapping previously shown.
source: We found WT 174 bp 5S yeast nucleosomes display a fully-wrapped side (position 158), and a side of partial unwrapping, in agreement with asymmetric 5S nucleosome unwrapping previously shown (Winogradoff and Aksimentiev, 2019; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ExoIII-S1 nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and by citations to prior work.

claim: WT nucleosomes displayed a much higher proportion of largely-wrapped species (≥135 bp) than did H3 R40A nucleosomes.
source: Here, WT nucleosomes displayed a much higher proportion of largely-wrapped species (≥135 bp) than did H3 R40A nucleosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ExoIII-S1 nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The mapping data support the hypothesis that RSC1 complexes manage partially-unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2 complexes.
source: Since RSC2 is more deficient than RSC1 in repositioning H3 R40A nucleosomes, the mapping supports the hypothesis that RSC1 complexes manage partially-unwrapped nucleosomes better than RSC2 complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the nuclease mapping and remodeling data.

claim: H3 R40A 5S nucleosomes are likely to have a distinct conformation that is not distinguished in the nuclease protection assay.
source: We note that H3 R40A 5S nucleosomes are likely to have a distinct conformation that is not distinguished in our nuclease protection assay, since remodeling by both RSC1 and (more so) by RSC2 complexes is inhibited by the H3 αN helix mutation (compare Figure 3E with Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that H3 R40A nucleosomes are remodeled less efficiently than WT nucleosomes.

claim: H3 R40A mutant octamers may enforce a greater degree of openness or distance between the 5S DNA ends, and thereby inhibit RSC activity.
source: These mutant octamers may enforce a greater degree of openness or distance between the 5S DNA ends, as demonstrated previously (Ferreira et al., 2007), and thereby inhibit RSC activity (perhaps the transition of binding to DNA translocation, see Discussion) – a nucleosome perturbation better managed by RSC1 complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which H3 R40A affects RSC activity, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hmo1 is an HMGB family protein that stabilizes fragile/partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, particularly at rRNA and ribosomal protein gene promoters.
source: Hmo1 is an HMGB family protein that stabilizes fragile/partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, particularly at rRNA and ribosomal protein gene promoters (Hall et al., 2006; Panday and Grove, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work characterizing Hmo1 function.

claim: Unlike other HMGB proteins which have an acidic CTD that promotes bending and nucleosome destabilization, Hmo1 is unique in containing a basic lysine rich C-terminal extension, and has been shown to stabilize chromatin and perform the functions of a linker histone.
source: Unlike other HMGB proteins which have an acidic CTD that promotes bending and nucleosome destabilization, Hmo1 is unique in containing a basic lysine rich C-terminal extension, and has been shown to stabilize chromatin and perform the functions of a linker histone (Panday and Grove, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work characterizing Hmo1 structure and function.

claim: Hmo1 is proposed to bind near the nucleosome dyad and use its basic extension to bind linker DNA and prevent bending.
source: Hmo1 is proposed to bind near the nucleosome dyad and use its basic extension to bind linker DNA and prevent bending (Panday and Grove, 2017), which may also improve wrapping and thus cooperate with RSC1 or RSC2 to promote remodeling.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and includes speculation about how Hmo1 might cooperate with RSC.

claim: Synthetic phenotypes are observed in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants.
source: Notably, we observe synthetic phenotypes in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic interaction assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rsc1Δ hmo1Δ synthetic sickness suggests a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
source: Notably, we observe synthetic phenotypes in rsc1Δ hmo1Δ mutants, but not rsc2Δ hmo1Δ mutants (Figure 4A), suggesting a greater reliance of Rsc2 on Hmo1 for functional cooperativity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data.

claim: The rsc1Δ hmo1Δ synthetic sickness is partially complemented by the presence of the Rsc1 CT2, and partially suppressed by high-copy RSC3 or RSC30.
source: Furthermore, as we saw with the H3 αN helix mutations, this synthetic sickness was partially complemented by the presence of the Rsc1 CT2, and partially suppressed by high-copy RSC3 or RSC30, providing further support that these proteins work together in a modular manner (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from complementation and suppression assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both Rsc1 and Rsc2 co-immunoprecipitate with Hmo1, which represents either a direct interaction between Hmo1 and RSC or colocalization on the same nucleosome(s).
source: Immunoprecipitation with anti-Myc or anti-V5 antibody followed by immunoblot analysis revealed that both Rsc1 and Rsc2 co-immunoprecipitate with Hmo1, which represents either a direct interaction between Hmo1 and RSC or colocalization on the same nucleosome(s) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hmo1 shows physical interaction on chromatin with Rsc1 and Rsc2, but strong functional/genetic interaction primarily with Rsc2.
source: Taken together, Hmo1 shows physical interaction on chromatin with Rsc1 and Rsc2, but strong functional/genetic interaction primarily with Rsc2 (RSC2 complexes are reliant on Hmo1, in a rsc1Δ strain).
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the co-IP and genetic interaction data.

claim: Hmo1 stimulates the sliding activity of RSC and SWI/SNF complex in vitro on 601 nucleosomes.
source: Hmo1 stimulates the sliding activity of RSC and SWI/SNF complex in vitro on 601 nucleosomes (Hepp et al., 2014), but it is not known whether stimulation applies equally to RSC1 and RSC2 complexes, or has a differential effect on their action upon partially-unwrapped nucleosomes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hmo1 moderately stimulates RSC1 activity, whereas Hmo1 greatly stimulates RSC2 activity on 5S nucleosomes.
source: Interestingly, Hmo1 moderately stimulates RSC1 activity, whereas Hmo1 greatly stimulates RSC2 activity (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for quantification), a property that is even more evident in conditions of limiting remodeler or at early time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays with Hmo1 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both RSC1 and RSC2 slide the 5S nucleosome at lower remodeler concentrations in the presence of Hmo1.
source: Moreover, both RSC1 and RSC2 slide the 5S nucleosome at lower remodeler concentrations in the presence of Hmo1 (30 nM RSC without Hmo1 compare with 10 nM RSC with Hmo1), further supporting a role for Hmo1 in stimulating RSC remodeling activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays with Hmo1 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both displayed robust sliding activity with 601 nucleosomes, with RSC1 activity slightly higher.
source: Here, RSC1 and RSC2 complexes both displayed robust sliding activity with 601 nucleosomes, with RSC1 activity slightly higher (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for quantification).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is a correlation between ejection and the use of strong positioning sequences – their initial stability from favored 'phasing' may convert to high instability and disfavored 'phasing' after 5 bp of DNA translocation – which may underlie the progressive ejection observed with 601 nucleosomes.
source: We note a correlation here and in prior work (Clapier et al., 2016) between ejection and the use of strong positioning sequences – their initial stability from favored 'phasing' may convert to high instability and disfavored 'phasing' after 5 bp of DNA translocation – which may underlie the progressive ejection observed with 601 nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of nucleosome ejection, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 was observed.
source: Indeed, we found robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 6 for quantification), and (by nuclease susceptibility) found that these nucleosomes remain largely wrapped (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleosome sliding assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes remain largely wrapped.
source: Indeed, we found robust remodeling of 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes by RSC2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 6 for quantification), and (by nuclease susceptibility) found that these nucleosomes remain largely wrapped (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nuclease mapping shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: While the H3 R40A mutation can result in an open and more loosely wrapped nucleosome conformation, this can be overcome by a strong DNA positioning sequence.
source: Our data support the model that while the H3 R40A mutation can result in an open and more loosely wrapped nucleosome conformation, this can be overcome by a strong DNA positioning sequence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes are remodeled efficiently by RSC2 and remain largely wrapped.

claim: The αN helix H3 R40A mutation itself does not impair remodeling by RSC2 unless that mutation confers partial unwrapping due to the underlying DNA sequence.
source: In addition, the data indicate that the αN helix H3 R40A mutation itself does not impair remodeling by RSC2 unless that mutation confers partial unwrapping due to the underlying DNA sequence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of RSC2 remodeling of 5S H3 R40A nucleosomes (poor remodeling) versus 601 H3 R40A nucleosomes (robust remodeling).

claim: The mapping data confirm that 5S nucleosomes produced with yeast octamers are less well-wrapped than 601 nucleosomes, and have DNA ends that are more susceptible to nuclease digestion.
source: Lastly, our mapping data confirm that 5S nucleosomes produced with yeast octamers are less well-wrapped than 601 nucleosomes, and have DNA ends that are more susceptible to nuclease digestion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nuclease mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: RSC has been examined by chromatin co-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) in several formats.
source: RSC has been examined by chromatin co-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) in several formats (Damelin et al., 2002; Yen et al., 2012; Vinayachandran et al., 2018; Brahma and Henikoff, 2019), though only one study has examined Rsc1/2 differences.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An early ChIP approach with microarrays examined Rsc1 and Rsc2 differences, and revealed similar promoter targets for RSC1 and RSC2 complexes.
source: This early ChIP approach with microarrays examined Rsc1 and Rsc2 differences, and revealed similar promoter targets for RSC1 and RSC2 complexes (Ng et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Recent examination of Sth1/RSC occupancy by the 'cut and run' MNase approach revealed general enrichment for RSC complexes at many +1 and −1 nucleosomes, as well as high enrichment of RSC within the NDR of genes with very wide NDRs (e.g., ribosomal protein genes).
source: Recent examination of Sth1/RSC occupancy by the 'cut and run' MNase approach (which would have superimposed and not distinguished between Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy) revealed general enrichment for RSC complexes at many +1 and −1 nucleosomes, as well as high enrichment of RSC within the NDR of genes with very wide NDRs (e.g., ribosomal protein genes).
evidence: This statement is based on prior work and is supported by the citation context.

claim: Wide NDR regions/promoters have been shown to contain RSC bound to partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, rather than the complete lack of nucleosomes.
source: Notably, these wide NDR regions/promoters have been shown to contain RSC bound to partially-unwrapped nucleosomes, rather than the complete lack of nucleosomes (Brahma and Henikoff, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RSC (Rsc1, Rsc2 and Rsc3) shows high occupancy at promoters with wide NDRs, with Rsc1 appearing more enriched than Rsc2.
source: First, we observed high occupancy of RSC (Rsc1, Rsc2 and Rsc3; Figure 5A) at promoters with wide NDRs, with Rsc1 appearing more enriched than Rsc2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hmo1 occupancy positively correlates with regions displaying the widest NDRs and bearing the highest Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy, with an apparent higher correlation with Rsc1.
source: Notably, Hmo1 occupancy positively correlates with regions displaying the widest NDRs and bearing the highest Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy, with an apparent higher correlation with Rsc1 (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The loci with the highest Hmo1 occupancy displayed a mean region size of 336 bp, and a remarkable two-thirds of those genes were ribosomal protein genes (RPGs).
source: The loci with the highest Hmo1 occupancy displayed a mean region size of 336 bp, and a remarkable two-thirds of those genes were ribosomal protein genes (RPGs).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Ribosomal protein gene promoters contain GC-rich sequences within their 'NDR' region, and Rsc3 enrichment is observed, consistent with Rsc3/30 involvement in targeting or retention.
source: Ribosomal protein gene promoters contain GC-rich sequences within their 'NDR' region, and in keeping, we observe Rsc3 enrichment, consistent with Rsc3/30 involvement in targeting or retention.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5A and by established knowledge about RPG promoter sequences.

claim: Rsc1 complexes are markedly more enriched than Rsc2 complexes at tDNAs.
source: The most striking difference between Rsc1 and Rsc2 occupancy was observed at tDNAs. tDNAs encode tRNAs, and are approximately the size of a single nucleosome - though they are among the most nucleosome-depleted loci in the yeast genome, due at least in part to the action of RSC (Parnell et al., 2008) and their high fractional occupancy by RNA polymerase III transcription factors (Kumar and Bhargava, 2013). Here, Rsc1 complexes are markedly more enriched than Rsc2 complexes, and Hmo1 is notably absent (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Hmo1 is notably absent at tDNAs.
source: Here, Rsc1 complexes are markedly more enriched than Rsc2 complexes, and Hmo1 is notably absent (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Many tDNAs are flanked by highly AT-rich sequences.
source: Notably, many tDNAs are flanked by highly AT-rich sequences (Giuliodori et al., 2003), which could (in principle) confer partial unwrapping during the uncommon times (e.g., after replication) when tDNAs are transiently unoccupied by Pol III; here, RSC1 complexes might conduct nucleosome sliding to reveal tDNA sequences to the Pol III machinery.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and includes speculation about the role of RSC1 at tDNAs.

claim: The high fractional occupancy of Pol III complexes likely underlies the lack of Hmo1 at tDNAs, as Pol III factors would likely compete with Hmo1 for DNA binding and can remove nucleosomes during transcription.
source: Indeed, the high fractional occupancy of Pol III complexes likely underlies the lack of Hmo1 at tDNAs, as Pol III factors would likely compete with Hmo1 for DNA binding and can remove nucleosomes during transcription.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Hmo1 is absent at tDNAs, which are highly occupied by Pol III.

claim: Modest differences in transcriptional profiles are observed between WT, rsc1Δ, and rsc2Δ.
source: We observe modest differences in transcriptional profiles between WT, rsc1Δ, and rsc2Δ (Figure 5G–H), which we interpret to be reflective of the known redundancy between Rsc1 and Rsc2 for most functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Combining rsc1∆ or rsc2∆ with hmo1∆ resulted in a strong transcriptional shift, resulting in the upregulation (>2 fold) and downregulation (>2 fold) of ~1000 genes.
source: However, combining rsc1∆ or rsc2∆ with hmo1∆ resulted in a strong transcriptional shift, resulting in the upregulation (>2 fold) and downregulation (>2 fold) of ~1000 genes (Figure 5G), with the most affected class of genes including RPGs, which are downregulated (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The most affected class of genes in rsc1∆ hmo1∆ and rsc2∆ hmo1∆ double mutants includes RPGs, which are downregulated.
source: However, combining rsc1∆ or rsc2∆ with hmo1∆ resulted in a strong transcriptional shift, resulting in the upregulation (>2 fold) and downregulation (>2 fold) of ~1000 genes (Figure 5G), with the most affected class of genes including RPGs, which are downregulated (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The transcriptional shift observed in the double mutants largely mirrors the shift of both up-regulation and down-regulation observed in response to environmental stress response (ESR) genes.
source: Additionally the transcriptional shift observed in the double mutants largely mirrors the shift of both up-regulation and down-regulation observed in response to environmental stress response (ESR) genes (Gasch et al., 2000; Brion et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and by citations to prior work defining ESR genes.

claim: Rsc1 and Rsc2 both cooperate with Hmo1 to promote the transcription of ribosomal protein genes.
source: These results suggest that Rsc1 and Rsc2 both cooperate with Hmo1 to promote the transcription of ribosomal protein genes, and that the burden for chromatin remodeling at these and other growth regulated loci requires the action of both Rsc1 and Rsc2, if Hmo1 is absent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data showing downregulation of RPGs in double mutants.

claim: The burden for chromatin remodeling at RPGs and other growth regulated loci requires the action of both Rsc1 and Rsc2, if Hmo1 is absent.
source: These results suggest that Rsc1 and Rsc2 both cooperate with Hmo1 to promote the transcription of ribosomal protein genes, and that the burden for chromatin remodeling at these and other growth regulated loci requires the action of both Rsc1 and Rsc2, if Hmo1 is absent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data showing strong transcriptional effects only in double mutants.

claim: Only rsc2∆ rsc30∆ mutants strongly impact RP genes.
source: Remarkably, only rsc2∆ rsc30∆ mutants strongly impact RP genes – suggesting that the RSC1 complex, which interacts more strongly with Rsc3/30, is more reliant on Rsc3/30 than is the RSC2 complex, and that in a rsc2∆ rsc30∆ both complexes are impaired (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The RSC1 complex, which interacts more strongly with Rsc3/30, is more reliant on Rsc3/30 than is the RSC2 complex.
source: Remarkably, only rsc2∆ rsc30∆ mutants strongly impact RP genes – suggesting that the RSC1 complex, which interacts more strongly with Rsc3/30, is more reliant on Rsc3/30 than is the RSC2 complex, and that in a rsc2∆ rsc30∆ both complexes are impaired (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data and the biochemical data showing differential Rsc3/30 association.

claim: In a rsc2∆ rsc30∆ mutant, both RSC1 and RSC2 complexes are impaired.
source: Remarkably, only rsc2∆ rsc30∆ mutants strongly impact RP genes – suggesting that the RSC1 complex, which interacts more strongly with Rsc3/30, is more reliant on Rsc3/30 than is the RSC2 complex, and that in a rsc2∆ rsc30∆ both complexes are impaired (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data.

claim: A whole genome duplication (WGD) occurred within the Saccharomyces lineage approximately 150 million years ago, resulting in RSC1/2 paralogs.
source: A whole genome duplication (WGD) occurred within the Saccharomyces lineage approximately 150 million years ago (Wolfe and Shields, 1997) resulting in RSC1/2 paralogs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on yeast genome evolution.

claim: The single RSC1/2 ortholog present in species that did not undergo the WGD is more closely related to RSC2 than RSC1, suggesting RSC2 as the more ancient ortholog.
source: We find the single RSC1/2 ortholog present in species that did not undergo the WGD (e.g., Zygosaccharomyces, Ashbya, and Lachancea), more closely related to RSC2 than RSC1, suggesting RSC2 as the more ancient ortholog (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Species more distant to S. cerevisiae lack both RSC3 and RSC30.
source: Notably, species more distant to S. cerevisiae lack both RSC3 and RSC30.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Following the appearance of RSC3, the WGD event then created RSC1/2 and RSC3/RSC30 orthologs, along with duplications of the ribosomal protein genes, a large fraction of which have been maintained in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Following the appearance of RSC3, the WGD event then created RSC1/2 and RSC3/RSC30 orthologs, along with duplications of the ribosomal protein genes, a large fraction of which have been maintained in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge about yeast genome evolution.

claim: HMO1 predates the appearance of RSC3 and the WGD and is found in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: Finally, HMO1 predates the appearance of RSC3 and the WGD and is found in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Albert et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Specialization of Rsc1 to preferentially bind Rsc3/30 and play a role in the regulation of the ribosomal protein genes was enabled by the WGD, and may have arisen to help rapidly and properly regulate RPGs in response to growth conditions.
source: Thus, specialization of Rsc1 to preferentially bind Rsc3/30 and play a role in the regulation of the ribosomal protein genes was enabled by the WGD, and may have arisen to help rapidly and properly regulate RPGs in response to growth conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary significance of Rsc1 specialization.

claim: RSC1 complexes bear a higher intrinsic ability to mobilize partially-unwrapped nucleosomes compared to RSC2.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with RSC1 complexes bearing a higher intrinsic ability to mobilize partially-unwrapped nucleosomes compared to RSC2, augmented by partner proteins that preferentially assist either RSC1 (Rsc3/30) or RSC2 (Hmo1) complexes to more efficiently remodel at locations with partially-wrapped nucleosomes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Partner proteins preferentially assist either RSC1 (Rsc3/30) or RSC2 (Hmo1) complexes to more efficiently remodel at locations with partially-wrapped nucleosomes.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with RSC1 complexes bearing a higher intrinsic ability to mobilize partially-unwrapped nucleosomes compared to RSC2, augmented by partner proteins that preferentially assist either RSC1 (Rsc3/30) or RSC2 (Hmo1) complexes to more efficiently remodel at locations with partially-wrapped nucleosomes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript.
